title: Can we achieve multiple inheritance in Java, why is multiple class inheritance disallowed (the diamond problem), and how do interfaces work around it?
shortTitle: Multiple inheritance — why class inheritance disallowed (diamond problem), interfaces as workaround
topicTitle: Can we achieve multiple inheritance in Java, why is multiple class inheritance d

s1_definition.profdef: Java does NOT allow a class to extend more than one class (`class X extends A, B` is illegal). The reason: the DIAMOND PROBLEM — if class A and class B both extend class C and both override a method `doWork()`, and class X extends both A and B, which version of `doWork()` does X inherit? A's or B's? The compiler cannot decide — ambiguity. Java solves this by allowing multiple INTERFACE implementation: `class X implements A, B`. If both interfaces have a default method with the same signature, the class MUST override it to resolve the conflict explicitly. Interfaces avoid the diamond problem because: (1) pre-Java-8 interfaces had no method bodies — no ambiguity. (2) Java 8+ default methods: if two interfaces provide the same default method, the implementing class MUST override to choose. The class is in control — no silent ambiguity.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh works at TWO departments: Trading AND Compliance. Both departments have a procedure called `processEndOfDay()`. Trading's version: "Close all open positions." Compliance's version: "Generate regulatory report." If Rajesh inherits BOTH — which one does he follow at end of day? AMBIGUOUS! Java prevents this by saying: "You can only belong to ONE department (single class inheritance)." BUT you can hold MULTIPLE LICENSES (interfaces): Trading License says "you MUST be able to close positions," Compliance License says "you MUST be able to generate reports." Rajesh implements BOTH — but HE decides how to do each one. No ambiguity.
s1_definition.oneliner: No multiple class inheritance (diamond problem — ambiguous method resolution). YES multiple interface implementation (class resolves conflicts explicitly). If two interfaces have same default method → implementing class MUST override.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Java does NOT allow a class to extend more than one class (`class X extends A, B` is illegal). The reason: the DIAMOND PROBLEM — if class A and class B both extend class C and both override a method `doWork()`, and class X extends both A and B, which version of `doWork()` does X inherit? A's or B's? The compiler cannot decide — ambiguity. Java solves this by allowing multiple INTERFACE implementation: `class X implements A, B`. If both interfaces have a default method with the same signature, the class MUST override it to resolve the conflict explicitly. Interfaces avoid the diamond problem because: (1) pre-Java-8 interfaces had no method bodies — no ambiguity. (2) Java 8+ default methods: if two interfaces provide the same default method, the implementing class MUST override to choose. The class is in control — no silent ambiguity.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh works at TWO departments: Trading AND Compliance. Both departments have a procedure called `processEndOfDay()`. Trading's version: "Close all open positions." Compliance's version: "Generate regulatory report." If Rajesh inherits BOTH — which one does he follow at end of day? AMBIGUOUS! Java prevents this by saying: "You can only belong to ONE department (single class inheritance)." BUT you can hold MULTIPLE LICENSES (interfaces): Trading License says "you MUST be able to close positions," Compliance License says "you MUST be able to generate reports." Rajesh implements BOTH — but HE decides how to do each one. No ambiguity.

**One line to remember:** No multiple class inheritance (diamond problem — ambiguous method resolution). YES multiple interface implementation (class resolves conflicts explicitly). If two interfaces have same default method → implementing class MUST override.

sections.s3_banking: **Problem — The bank's TradingService needs capabilities from TWO interfaces:** Tradable (execute trades, get market) and Auditable (generate audit report, get market). BOTH interfaces have a default method `getMarket()` with different returns — Tradable says "NSE", Auditable says "BSE". The developer first tried `class TradingService extends TradingDepartment, AuditDepartment` — compile error (multiple class inheritance). The fix: make Tradable and Auditable interfaces. TradingService implements both. For the conflicting `getMarket()`, the class overrides and combines both: "NSE + BSE".

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1.** TradingService extends BaseService (ONE class) + implements Tradable + Auditable (TWO interfaces). Multiple interface implementation: allowed. Multiple class inheritance: forbidden.

**Step 2.** Tradable has `default getMarket()` → "NSE". Auditable has `default getMarket()` → "BSE". SAME signature, DIFFERENT implementations. CONFLICT!

**Step 3.** TradingService MUST override getMarket(). Without override: compile error "inherits unrelated defaults." The class uses `Tradable.super.getMarket()` + `Auditable.super.getMarket()` to combine both: "NSE + BSE".

**Step 4.** BaseService has `getServiceType()` → "BASE_SERVICE". Tradable has default `getServiceType()` → "TRADING". Auditable has default `getServiceType()` → "AUDIT". Three-way conflict? NO — class method ALWAYS wins over interface defaults. `service.getServiceType()` → "BASE_SERVICE" without any override needed.

**Step 5.** Resolution priority: (1) class method wins over everything, (2) sub-interface default wins over super-interface, (3) if two unrelated interfaces conflict → class MUST override. No silent ambiguity at any level.
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ THE DIAMOND PROBLEM (why multiple class inheritance is banned) ═══

           Vehicle
          /       \
    Electric     Gas
    start()→A   start()→B
          \       /
          Hybrid    ← which start()? A or B? AMBIGUOUS! ❌

  ═══ JAVA'S SOLUTION: multiple INTERFACE implementation ═══

    Tradable          Auditable
    getMarket()→NSE   getMarket()→BSE
          \             /
       TradingService
       @Override getMarket() → "NSE + BSE"  ✅ RESOLVED BY CLASS!

  ═══ RESOLUTION PRIORITY ═══

  1. CLASS method wins over ALL interface defaults (no override needed)
  2. Sub-interface default wins over super-interface
  3. Two unrelated interface defaults → class MUST override (compile error otherwise)

  ═══ InterfaceName.super.method() ═══

  Tradable.super.getMarket()   → "NSE"   (delegate to Tradable's default)
  Auditable.super.getMarket()  → "BSE"   (delegate to Auditable's default)
  // Class combines: "NSE + BSE" — explicit, clear, no ambiguity
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Java disallows multiple class inheritance to prevent the diamond problem: if class A and class B both override a method from class C, and class X extends both A and B, the compiler cannot determine which version X inherits — ambiguity. Java allows multiple interface implementation instead. If two interfaces have abstract methods with the same signature, the class simply provides one implementation that satisfies both. If two interfaces have conflicting DEFAULT methods, the compiler forces the class to override and explicitly resolve the conflict — no silent ambiguity.

In my banking service, TradingService implements Tradable (default getMarket → "NSE") and Auditable (default getMarket → "BSE"). Without overriding getMarket(), the compiler reports "inherits unrelated defaults." The class resolves it using `InterfaceName.super.method()` syntax: `Tradable.super.getMarket()` returns "NSE", `Auditable.super.getMarket()` returns "BSE", and the class combines them. For the getServiceType() conflict, the class-wins rule applies: BaseService.getServiceType() ("BASE_SERVICE") automatically wins over both interface defaults — no override needed.

The resolution priority: class method always wins over interface defaults. Sub-interface default wins over super-interface default. Two unrelated interface defaults with the same signature require the implementing class to override. This design ensures that multiple inheritance of behavior (through interface default methods) is safe — conflicts are always resolved explicitly by the programmer, never silently by the compiler.
